title: I built a browser bullet-hell MMO (Realm of the Mad God style) almost entirely with Claude Code. Here's what worked, what didn't, and where I still had to step in
author: Business-Ad2503
selftext:
I've been making Sunward, a pixel-art bullet-hell MMO you play in the browser: four heroes, huge procedurally generated islands, permadeath, parties, trading, dungeons and random encounters in every biome. Almost all of the code was written by AI, mostly Claude Code, while I directed, playtested and made the design calls. I wanted to share how that actually went, because it wasn't the "type one prompt, get a game" story.

How it was built. I started the project in Codex, then moved to Claude Code, which wrote most of the game. Later sessions ran in Claude Code's cloud mode, working straight on my GitHub repo: it opens a pull request for each change and merges it, and I pull it onto the server with one command. The art is from PixelLab (characters and enemies) and Higgsfield (the UI kit), and the sound is from CC0 packs. The server is plain Node with WebSockets on a Hetzner server that costs a few euros a month. Claude also wrote the deployment script (HTTPS, firewall, backups) and walked me through setting up the server step by step, which I'd never done before.

What surprised me in a good way. It was great at the "boring but hard" parts. A security review found a real item-duplication exploit in trading (reconnecting mid-trade let you keep the item and give it away). It wrote a chat filter and when exploring felt laggy, it benchmarked the ground renderer, found each new patch of ground was freezing the game for about 100 ms, and rewrote it to paint in small slices. It even filmed the clips in this post itself, by running the game in a headless browser.

Where it struggled. Visual bugs it couldn't see. My Esc key wouldn't open the settings menu, and it took three attempts: the first fix solved a different real bug, and only when I said "it closes the menu but won't open it" did it work out that the browser was closing the dialog the instant it opened. My heroes also "jumped" when turning, and it turned out the sprite tool draws the running animation at a different size for each direction; it only found that once it measured every frame. And when things felt laggy, it spent a while checking the server before we worked out it was my 4G home internet (a cafe fixed it instantly).

What I learned. The AI is only as good as my bug descriptions and screenshots. "It's laggy" got me nowhere; "144 fps, 195 ms ping" plus a quick ping test solved it in minutes. The biggest skill wasn't prompting, it was being a good tester and saying exactly what I saw.

Try it: [https://playsunward.com](https://playsunward.com/). It's free, no download, and you can play as a guest in seconds. It's early access, so press F9 in game to send a bug report or feedback, or comment here.

I'm curious how others here handle playtesting with AI-written code, especially visual and "feel" issues the AI can't see for itself. And if you try it, I'd love to hear what feels good and what's broken.
